source.title: Constraint Breeds Generalization: Temporal Dynamics as an Inductive Bias

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper and appendix; no apparent truncation or document mismatch.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports its own results on cross-encoding transfer and transfer to unseen physical regimes. These are out-of-distribution settings, which the claim excludes from its versions.
record.gate_note: The study tests out-of-distribution transfer and representation stability, not the versions’ in-distribution train/test-gap claims. Reported cross-encoding patterns and measured correlates are recorded under fits_no_version. Cited findings are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The study tests temporal dissipation, cross-encoding transfer, receptive-field structure and zero-shot RL transfer, but none of V1–V8. It does not compare random with natural labels, sweep width, compare convolutional with fully connected classifiers, compare optimizers or batch sizes, manipulate dropout, measure magnitude-aware sharpness, or remove memorized examples. Its PAC-Bayesian analysis reports held-out errors and gaps, but does not test any named version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate: the authors argue that suitably constrained temporal dissipation, particularly transition regimes, promotes invariant representations, structured receptive fields and zero-shot transfer. They attribute the benefit to matching temporal integration with signal dynamics rather than memory capacity alone.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses spiking neural networks, temporally encoded inputs, and transfer to unseen encodings or physical regimes; the claim versions concern natural-label in-distribution generalization and other named interventions or measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Cross-encoding outcome varies by architecture and training encoding regime. In RL, transfer varies with membrane leak β and task; the paper reports instability for over-constrained regimes and degraded transfer for β = 1.0 on complex tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: SNN cross-encoding transfer depends on the training encoding. Strongly expansive encodings transfer poorly to positive δ, whereas transition and dissipative encodings support broader, asymmetric transfer.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Temporal encoding regimes influence cross-encoding transfer in the tested SNN classifier.

fits_no_version.finding: The architecture comparisons show encoding-dependent transfer failures and successes; Avg-Pool MLP supports broad transfer in several regimes, with substantial variability in some conditions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architecture and temporal aggregation affect cross-encoding transfer.

fits_no_version.finding: Across 1440 encoding-pair/run observations, firing-rate CV correlates negatively with accuracy: −0.783, −0.602 and −0.215 for Layers 1–3.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Lower firing-rate variability correlates with higher cross-encoding accuracy in this SNN experiment.

fits_no_version.finding: Layer 3 CV is 0.470 ± 0.288 under expansive training and 0.307 ± 0.051 under dissipative training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Temporal training regimes affect representation variability in the tested SNN.

record.problems: The reported transfer settings are out-of-distribution and do not address the in-distribution claim versions. Some cross-encoding architecture comparisons are stated qualitatively in the main text; the detailed appendix tables are flattened in the supplied text, limiting reliable assignment of individual matrix values. The paper reports means and standard deviations for several experiments, but the selected CV correlations are not accompanied by confidence intervals.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports many additional cross-encoding matrix entries, RL agent/task/β combinations, receptive-field conditions, and PAC-Bayes metrics. They were left out because the version list concerns in-distribution generalization and the reported outcomes are cross-encoding/OOD transfer, feature structure, or optimization metrics. Detailed numeric cross-encoding matrices appear in Appendix Tables 5–9; RL results appear in Tables 2–3 and 17; feature-structure results appear in Tables 1 and 12–13; PAC-Bayes results appear in Tables 18–19.

untested.parts: Coexistence of fixed-random-label fitting and natural-label held-out generalization, including chance performance on held-out random labels.
Test-error changes when widening beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected classification accuracy and the contribution of learned local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer performance under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and compensating recipe changes.
Dropout effects on held-out error and interactions with data size, augmentation and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware weight-perturbation sharpness versus generalization gaps and competing norm or margin measures.
Test-accuracy effects of removing highly memorized examples compared with random removal.

record.verdict_notes: Replace the record's tests/T3 classification with discusses/T6. The mismatch is with the specific interventions, comparisons and measures in V1–V8; OOD evaluation alone is not a universal exclusion rule. Appendix A.4 does report in-distribution test errors and train/test gaps, contrary to the record's blanket characterization, but KL divergence and gradient variability do not test V7. Additional experiments are already declared in rows_left_out and supply no missing version-specific results.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization alongside natural-label test accuracy; named models and datasets in the version.
Width sweep beyond interpolation on natural labels.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizer comparisons on held-out performance.
Large-batch comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and recipe changes.
Dropout effects on held-out error and interactions with training-set size or augmentation.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness and its relationship to the in-distribution training/test gap.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting natural-label test accuracy.

rows.subject: SNN
rows.operation_detail: Cross-encoding accuracy across training and test dynamical regimes; text reports the pattern by training regime.
rows.value: high ID accuracy but performance collapses immediately when δtest > 0
rows.locator: Section 2.2, Asymmetric Generalization Landscapes; Appendix Tables 5–9
rows.note: The paper describes cross-encoding transfer, not held-out examples from the same distribution.
rows.check: Cross-encoding accuracy measures none of the versions. The reported collapse overgeneralizes across expansive training: Table 5 shows δtrain = −0.3 retains 92.4% at δtest = 0.3 and 76.8% at δtest = 10; the severe collapse principally concerns δtrain = −1.5 and −1.0.

rows.value: maintaining high accuracy across the entire δtest axis; transition zone achieves the strongest overall generalization
rows.check: Cross-encoding transfer measures none of the versions. The qualitative plateau is supported, but accuracy is not uniformly maintained at its diagonal level: δtrain = 2 has 94.2% diagonal accuracy versus 70.9% at δtest = −1.5.

rows.subject: LSTM, RNN, and MLP (Last-T)
rows.operation_detail: Cross-encoding accuracy compared with the SNN.

conditions.value: tested away from the training diagonal

rows.note: The text reports these architectures together; no separate numeric outcomes are given here.
rows.check: The grouped architecture comparison measures none of the versions and should be separated by model and encoding condition. Universal off-diagonal failure is inconsistent with Tables 7–9; for example, LSTM trained at δ = 5 retains 89.4% at δtest = 10, and Last-T MLP trained at δ = 10 retains 91.0% at δtest = −1.5.

rows.subject: MLP (Avg-Pool)
rows.value: partial generalization with significantly higher volatility (wider confidence bands)
rows.note: The paper attributes this transfer pattern to collapsing temporal variation before learning; that explanation is not separately measured here.
rows.check: The transfer and run-to-run variability measures bear on none of the versions. Partial transfer is condition-dependent: Table 6 includes broad high-accuracy transfer for several training encodings and severe failures for others. Reported deviations are standard deviations, not an identified statistical test of higher volatility.
